neurological_exam.additional: Tacrolimus trough levels: target 8-12 ng/mL; average 10.5 ± 4.1 ng/mL over 3 months. No history of tacrolimus toxicity (no elevated levels). No recent infections, immunizations, or new medications. CMV PCR serum: negative. EBV PCR serum: negative. Brain MRI: normal. Insidious onset over 2 weeks distinguishes from acute GBS — but 4-week total disease duration still meets GBS criteria.

patient.chief_complaint: Two-week progressive lower extremity weakness with dizziness and difficulty walking, 4 months after bilateral lung transplant on triple immunosuppression.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 66-year-old bilateral lung transplant recipient presenting 4 months post-transplant with a 2-week history of progressive lower extremity weakness. He underwent uncomplicated bilateral lung transplantation 4 months ago for end-stage COPD. His immunosuppression regimen is tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone, with tacrolimus levels consistently therapeutic at 10.5 ng/mL on average over 3 months. He reports no recent infections, new medications, immunizations, or exposures. He denies respiratory illness or diarrheal illness. Two weeks ago he began noticing dizziness and generalized weakness with difficulty ambulating. The weakness has been specifically in his lower extremities and has progressed gradually — he initially needed a cane and now requires bilateral support. He has no upper extremity weakness and no sensory symptoms initially, though mild distal tingling developed in the second week. He initially had normal reflexes on exam, which became hypoactive and then absent at the ankles by week 3. This subacute 2-3 week progression on triple immunosuppression creates a challenging differential — tacrolimus polyneuropathy must be excluded (tacrolimus can cause demyelinating neuropathy), but levels are therapeutic and the progressive course is distinct. CMV and EBV (common post-transplant opportunistic infections) were tested and are negative. The diagnosis required nerve conduction studies and lumbar puncture to distinguish GBS from tacrolimus neuropathy and opportunistic infection neuropathy.

specialized_test.impression: Acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with axonal features. Increased distal motor latencies, reduced conduction velocities, decreased CMAP amplitudes, absent F-waves and H-reflexes bilaterally. Asymmetric left greater than right involvement. Reduced sural and ulnar sensory SNAP amplitudes. Findings meet electrodiagnostic criteria for acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

CMV PCR negative in serum and CSF; valganciclovir prophylaxis ongoing — CMV viremia prevented
Progression over 2-3 weeks at upper boundary for GBS — but single monophasic attack without relapse; post-transplant immune dysregulation likely trigger for acute GBS

critical_actions: Plasmapheresis is CONTRAINDICATED in solid organ transplant recipients — clears immunosuppressive medications (tacrolimus) and can precipitate acute rejection; IVIG is the ONLY appropriate GBS treatment here
Do NOT reduce tacrolimus without transplant team input — GBS does not require immunosuppression reduction; tacrolimus reduction risks rejection
CMV neuropathy must be excluded — CMV PCR serum and CSF are mandatory in post-transplant patients
Use non-sucrose IVIG formulation — baseline renal impairment from tacrolimus
NCS pattern distinguishes GBS from tacrolimus neuropathy: demyelinating with absent F-waves is GBS; distal axonal is tacrolimus
contraindicated_actions: Plasmapheresis — contraindicated in solid organ transplant
Reducing tacrolimus without transplant team guidance
key_reasoning_points: Plasmapheresis and GBS in organ transplant: plasmapheresis rapidly eliminates tacrolimus and other immunosuppressants, risking acute allograft rejection — IVIG is the only appropriate choice
Tacrolimus polyneuropathy: produces distal symmetric axonal neuropathy; does NOT cause the demyelinating pattern with absent F-waves and elevated CSF protein seen in GBS
Post-transplant immune dysregulation can trigger GBS even in an immunosuppressed patient — the transplant itself and the attendant immune perturbation may be the trigger
CSF protein elevation is not seen in tacrolimus neuropathy — albumino-cytologic dissociation is specific to GBS and helps distinguish the two
Therapeutic tacrolimus levels argue against tacrolimus toxicity as the cause — this was a critical data point

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Tacrolimus level 9.8 ng/mL is therapeutic; tacrolimus neuropathy is axonal not demyelinating; CSF protein elevation is not seen with tacrolimus; reducing tacrolimus risks rejection — IVIG is needed for GBS
